summary: All 16 units across 8 modules were read in full and every numeric key was recomputed (mg/kg doses, charcoal 1 g/kg, anion gap, MAP, Friedewald LDL, one-sixth breakthrough morphine, Cockcroft-Gault, rule of three, PRR, reporting rate, RR/ARR/NNT, AKI ratio, R ratio, PPV, BSA, ANC, VAF, Reid index, Nottingham score, Ki-67); all keys and tolerances are correct and all MCQ keys have exactly one defensible option. Naloxone duration (30 to 90 minutes), charcoal dose (50 g adult, 1 g/kg child, about 1 hour window), paracetamol, salicylate and flumazenil content are accurate, framed as teaching examples, and no unsafe treatment advice was found. Only six minor issues were found: a drug-class label, an over-simple breakthrough-dose rule, a missing flumazenil duration, an unsupported distractor, a linear fixation-time model and a Hayflick wording slip. Confidence is moderate to high, but this is an AI review only and the course still needs a subject-matter expert (clinical pathologist/pharmacologist) before clinical reliance. Note that tricyclic antidepressant overdose management is not taught in this course beyond its role as a flumazenil/charcoal caution.

issues.problem: The table row 'Thiazide-like diuretic (indapamide, bendroflumethiazide)' groups bendroflumethiazide, which is a thiazide-type diuretic, under thiazide-like; thiazide-like agents are indapamide and chlortalidone.
issues.suggestedFix: Label the row 'Thiazide and thiazide-like diuretics' or list indapamide and chlortalidone as the thiazide-like examples. Check wording against the BNF/NICE.

issues.problem: The lesson states 'Breakthrough dose approximately 1/6 x total 24-hour oral morphine dose' as 'a common palliative care rule' without qualification. UK palliative guidance gives one-tenth to one-sixth of the daily dose, with the dose individualised (for example in renal impairment). Q007 key (15 mg) is correct for the stated one-sixth rule.
issues.suggestedFix: State that breakthrough is typically one-tenth to one-sixth of the 24-hour dose, individualised and reviewed (lower in renal impairment or frailty), and keep the one-sixth calculation as the teaching example. Verify against current local palliative care guidance.

issues.problem: The objective asks students to match naloxone and flumazenil with their cautions, and the lesson gives the naloxone duration (30 to 90 minutes) but no flumazenil duration; the callout only says both are 'shorter-acting than many of the drugs they reverse', so the flumazenil re-sedation risk is not quantified.
issues.suggestedFix: Add that flumazenil's effect is also short (roughly 1 hour or less, source check recommended) compared with many benzodiazepines, so re-sedation can occur and observation is needed.

issues.problem: The distractor 'Gastric lavage routinely' is meant to be wrong, but the lesson never states that routine gastric lavage is not recommended; it only warns against induced vomiting. The key therefore relies on knowledge not taught.
issues.suggestedFix: Add a line to the lesson that routine gastric lavage is not recommended and is considered only on toxicology advice, or replace the distractor.

issues.problem: Fixation time is modelled linearly as t = d/v with 1 mm/h (10 mm liver slice = 5 h; Q007 14 mm kidney slice = 7 h). Formalin penetration is diffusion-limited and slows with depth (roughly proportional to the square root of time), so the linear model understates the time needed, and slices this thick are not recommended in practice (about 3 to 5 mm).
issues.suggestedFix: Unverified, recommend a source check. Either state that penetration slows with depth and the figures are only a rough lower bound, or use thinner slices (3 to 5 mm) with the advice to slice thinly. Keep Q007 key consistent with whichever model is chosen.

issues.problem: Stem says 'normal fibroblasts stop after about 50 passages'. The Hayflick limit is about 40 to 60 population doublings, not passages (a passage may cover several doublings).
issues.suggestedFix: Reword to 'after about 50 population doublings' for both the tumour cells and normal fibroblasts.
